conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for making time for this. I’m Dr. Ramirez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. Over the next few minutes we’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS—to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. It’s simply ten questions about the past seven days; there are no right or wrong answers, just whatever is true for you. Everything you share stays confidential, and my only goal is to be sure you feel heard and supported. Ready to begin?

1. Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Morning, Doctor. I guess I’ve still been able to laugh—like when the baby does that little startle in his sleep and throws his arms up. It makes me chuckle most times, so I’d say it hasn’t felt difficult at all.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, that sounds right—most days I still find things funny. Like yesterday my sister sent me a silly meme and I laughed out loud while I was feeding the baby.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I do look forward to stuff—like my morning coffee once the baby settles, or the little walk we take to the mailbox. They’re small things, but they feel nice.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Not really. If he spits up a ton after I feed him, I might think, “Maybe I burped him wrong,” but I don’t keep chewing on it. I just change us both and move on.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little, yeah. Like, I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly wonder if his breathing sounds “normal,” even though he’s right there in the bassinet perfectly fine. It’s not all day, just quick little waves that pass once I peek at him.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t had that panicky feeling—just the little worries about his breathing or temperature, but nothing that makes my heart race or feels like a real scare.
Things have been getting on top of me
Sometimes, yeah—like when he cluster-feeds and I can’t finish folding the laundry or make something decent to eat. I feel a bit swamped in the moment, but once he naps I catch back up and it’s okay.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, my mood hasn’t messed with my sleep. Once he’s down for the night I usually drift off pretty easily—maybe because I’m tired from the day, but I’m not lying there feeling unhappy or wired.
I have felt sad or miserable
Not really. I get a little teary when I’m extra tired, but it’s gone in a minute—nothing that hangs around or feels truly miserable.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t had that kind of crying. If I tear up it’s usually just because I’m tired, and it stops pretty quickly.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
Never. That hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 5: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, date not specified  
Instrument: Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale (EPDS) style clinical interview  

Symptoms endorsed:  
- Transient, situational worries about infant well-being (Q4)  
- Occasional feeling of being “swamped” with daily tasks (Q6)  

Symptoms denied:  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, excessive guilt, panic attacks, sleep disruption secondary to mood, crying spells, self-harm ideation (Q1-3,5-10)  

Pattern:  
- Maintains capacity for enjoyment and humor; momentary anxiety and coping strain are context-linked (cluster-feeding, fatigue) and resolve quickly. No pervasive depressive or anxiety features observed during interview.  

Risk screening:  
- No current indicators for major postpartum depression or anxiety disorder.  
- No self-harm or safety concerns identified.  

Overall observation:  
Screening responses do not suggest clinically significant postpartum depression or anxiety at this time. Continue routine paediatric and maternal follow-up; re-screen if mood, functioning, or safety status changes.
